paragraphs.heading: A group, not a single mineral
paragraphs.text: Feldspar is the name of a group of rock-forming minerals. They are aluminium tectosilicates, and they also contain other ingredients such as sodium, calcium, potassium or barium. The most common members are the plagioclase feldspars, which are the sodium-calcium ones, and the alkali feldspars, which are the potassium-sodium ones. By weight, feldspars make up about 60% of Earth's crust and 41% of its continental crust.

paragraphs.heading: Where feldspars turn up
paragraphs.text: Feldspars crystallize out of magma, and the igneous rocks they form in can be intrusive or extrusive. They are also present in many kinds of metamorphic rock and in many kinds of sedimentary rock. A rock made almost wholly of calcic plagioclase feldspar has a name of its own: anorthosite.

paragraphs.heading: Where the name comes from
paragraphs.text: The word comes from the German Feldspat, which joins Feld, meaning "field", and Spat, meaning "flake". Spat was an old word for a rock that splits easily into flakes. Feldspat came in during the 18th century as a more specific term. The ending changed to -spar under the influence of the English word spar, which means a non-opaque mineral with good cleavage.

paragraphs.heading: How the crystal is built
paragraphs.text: A feldspar crystal is based on units called aluminosilicate tetrahedra. Each tetrahedron is one aluminium or silicon ion with four oxygen ions around it. Every oxygen ion is shared with a neighbouring tetrahedron, and this sharing ties the units into a three-dimensional network. The network is open enough for other ions, typically sodium, potassium or calcium, to fit inside it and balance the charge.

paragraphs.heading: The order they form in
paragraphs.text: As magma cools, the feldspars do not all appear at once. Calcium-rich plagioclase crystallizes first. As crystallization goes on, the plagioclase becomes more and more sodium-rich. The last feldspar to crystallize from the magma is K-feldspar.

paragraphs.heading: From feldspar to clay
paragraphs.text: Chemical weathering breaks feldspars down by a process called hydrolysis, and the products are clay minerals, including illite, smectite and kaolinite. Hydrolysis starts with the feldspar dissolving in water. This works better in an acidic or basic solution than in a neutral one, and how fast the feldspar dissolves sets how fast it weathers. The dissolved feldspar then reacts with H⁺ or OH⁻ ions, and clays precipitate. Feldspars are so abundant in the crust that clays are very abundant products of weathering.

paragraphs.heading: A texture you can see
paragraphs.text: Perthite is a typical texture in alkali feldspar. It forms by exsolution: as a feldspar of in-between composition cools, it separates into feldspars of contrasting composition. In many granites these perthitic textures can be seen with the naked eye. Some feldspar of labradorite composition shows a play of colours, and this too is due to exsolution, in the form of very fine-grained lamellae known as Bøggild intergrowth.
